title: Causal Evidence for Emotion‐Selective Neural Populations Supporting Emotion Perception in the Human Third Visual Pathway
content:
State-dependent cortico-cortical paired associative stimulation was used to selectively potentiate pSTS→V1/V2 backward projections while participants viewed one target emotional expression. Strengthening the feedback route, but not the reverse V1/V2→pSTS route, selectively improved recognition of the target emotion. The findings provide causal evidence for emotion-selective neural populations embedded within backward projections of the human third visual pathway.


ABSTRACT

The posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) is central to social perception, but whether it contains emotion-selective neural populations that causally contribute to emotion recognition in humans remains unknown. Here, we used state-dependent cortico-cortical paired associative stimulation (ccPAS) to test whether emotion-selective populations within the human pSTS→V1/V2 re-entrant pathway can be selectively strengthened via Hebbian-like plasticity. Sixty participants received ccPAS targeting either backward (pSTS→V1/V2) or forward (V1/V2→pSTS) projections of the third visual pathway while viewing fearful or happy faces; only one emotion was temporally paired with stimulation. pSTS→V1/V2 ccPAS selectively improved recognition of the paired emotion, with no effects on the unpaired emotion or following V1/V2→pSTS stimulation. These findings provide causal evidence that spatially overlapping, but functionally distinct, emotion-selective neural populations within the human pSTS–V1/V2 pathway make specific contributions to emotion recognition, such that ccPAS strengthening of one population selectively improves recognition of its preferred emotion, highlighting the functional relevance and selective malleability of human pSTS–V1/V2 circuits for emotion recognition.
